strengths: Addresses a practically significant problem — layer selection and score aggregation for gradient-based influence functions — that is directly relevant given the computational cost of computing influence over full LLM parameter spaces.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning four models of varying scale (RoBERTa-Large, Llama-3.2 1B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B, Mistral 7B) and eight GLUE tasks, with 10-seed repetitions and a well-documented pipeline (Appendix A) that aids reproducibility.

The critique of the cancellation-effect metric (Yeh et al. 2022) is well-motivated: the paper shows that C(W) is not additive across parameter subsets and can obscure per-weight cancellation, and backs this with a theoretical counterexample as well as empirical Spearman correlations that are weak-to-absent across models.

The proposed Rank and Vote aggregation strategies are simple, intuitive, and empirically shown to improve downstream filtering performance (e.g., notable win-rate gains for DataInf/TracIn under Vote), providing an easy-to-adopt alternative to naive mean aggregation.

The Noise Detection Rate (NDR) and AUC metrics are a useful practical contribution aimed at reducing the cost of evaluating influence methods without requiring full retraining, and the paper empirically validates their correlation with downstream accuracy across settings.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result (Theorem 5.1) is not rigorously established: the proof by contradiction asserts, without formal justification, that 'universal anti-alignment is impossible' and concludes existence of a favorable validation point via informal appeal to gradient co-directionality; this weakens the claimed theoretical grounding for rejecting the cancellation-effect hypothesis.

The paper's main headline claim ('first is not really better than last', middle attention layers being generally superior) is not consistently supported by its own results: RoBERTa-Large favors later attention layers, Mistral/Qwen favor early-middle layers, and for Llama-3.2 1B no influence-based filtering configuration even outperforms random removal — this substantially undercuts the generality of the central narrative and is not adequately reconciled in the main text.

The correlation of the proposed NDR/AUC proxy metrics with downstream accuracy is only moderate (0.5–0.7) under standard mean/rank aggregation, and only becomes strong (0.8–0.9) when combined with the paper's own Vote aggregation method, entangling the contribution and making it unclear how reliable NDR is as a general-purpose proxy independent of the proposed aggregation scheme.

Statistical testing choices are relatively permissive (Wilcoxon p<0.1 with only 10 seeds) and effect-size thresholds (>1% change) are ad hoc, raising concerns about the robustness of significance claims underlying the aggregation strategy comparisons.

Experimental design choices (only 4500 training samples, uniform 20% label-flip noise injection, binarization of MNLI/STSB, LoRA-only fine-tuning) diverge from standard benchmark protocols and realistic noise distributions, raising questions about how well the findings generalize to real-world detrimental-sample detection or to full-parameter fine-tuning settings.

Related influence-estimation approaches beyond TracIn/DataInf/Cosine (e.g., EK-FAC/Kronecker-factored curvature methods used in Grosse et al. 2023) are not empirically compared, despite being cited as relevant scaled methods, limiting the generality of conclusions about layer choice across influence-function families.

Presentation is dense and appendix-heavy, with large result tables provided with limited synthesis or higher-level takeaways in the main text, making it harder for readers to extract actionable guidance despite the volume of experiments.

strengths: Broad empirical scope: experiments span four models of different scale/architecture (RoBERTa-Large, Llama-3.2 1B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B, Mistral 7B) and eight GLUE tasks, with 10 seeds per configuration, giving a large body of raw results (extensively documented in the appendices).

The paper tackles a genuinely under-studied question (which layers/aggregation strategies are best for LLM influence estimation) that has practical relevance for scaling influence functions to large models.

The proposed Rank/Vote aggregation strategies are simple, well-motivated by the observed low correlation between layer groups, and are shown to give measurable accuracy improvements in several settings (e.g., Mistral).

The NDR/AUC proxy-metric idea is a reasonable attempt to reduce the cost of evaluating influence methods without full retraining, and the correlation analysis in Table 2 is a useful empirical check on this idea.
weaknesses: The paper's central, title-defining claim ('first is not really better than last', 'middle attention layers are better') is not consistently supported by its own results: for Llama-3.2 1B, none of the influence-based configurations beat the trivial Random-removal baseline (Section 5.2, Table 5), directly undermining the generality of the main conclusion and contradicting the framing pushed in the abstract/conclusion.

The 'best' layer group varies substantially across models and methods (Table 3, Appendix C): RoBERTa favors later layers, Llama and Mistral favor early/middle layers, and there is no single coherent layer-selection rule offered, only post-hoc, model-specific observations. This weakens the paper's claim of having identified a general principle to replace Yeh et al.'s 'first is better' rule.

Theorem 5.1's proof is not rigorous: the derivation uses informal 'WLOG' simplifications, an unproven claim that 'universal anti-alignment is impossible,' and treats C(ω)→∞ as a literal limit while simultaneously invoking a small but nonzero ε, without clearly justified inequalities; the theorem only establishes existence of some validation point where cancellation helps, which is a weak (almost trivially true) counterexample-type result rather than a substantive theoretical contribution.

The empirical correlation evidence against the cancellation effect (Table 1, column ρ) is itself weak in both directions (mostly |ρ|<0.3), so the paper's own evidence for 'cancellation is unreliable' is only marginally stronger than the claim it is refuting; no confidence intervals, sample sizes, or significance levels are reported for these correlations.

NDR requires ground-truth knowledge of which samples are mislabeled, which is generally unavailable in real deployment scenarios where influence functions are actually needed (i.e., to find unknown detrimental samples). Its usefulness as an evaluation proxy for method development is plausible but its practical framing as solving the 'costly retraining' problem is somewhat overstated, since it substitutes one form of ground-truth requirement for another.

Correlations validating NDR/AUC as reliable proxies are only moderate (0.5–0.7 under mean aggregation) and become strong only under Vote aggregation, meaning the very metric proposed to avoid retraining is itself only reliable when paired with the paper's own novel aggregation method — a somewhat circular support structure with limited evidence of standalone generalizability.

Experimental setup restricts LoRA fine-tuning to query/value projections and a small number of training/validation/test samples (≤4500/500/500), and injects synthetic uniform label noise rather than realistic detrimental data (e.g., adversarial poisoning, distribution shift, subtle mislabeling), which may limit how representative the findings are of real-world data influence/auditing use cases.

The comparison set of influence functions is narrow (TracIn, Cosine, DataInf, and Yeh et al.'s WE-based variants); stronger recent second-order methods mentioned in related work (e.g., EK-FAC/Kronecker-factored approximations, Arnoldi iteration) are not empirically compared, despite being natural baselines given the paper's stated goal of understanding scalable influence estimation.

Statistical testing relies on only 10 seeds with Wilcoxon tests and an arbitrary 1% mean-change threshold for 'significance' in the Rank/Vote comparisons, which is a fairly weak basis for the many fine-grained claims made throughout Section 5.3 and the appendix tables.

The paper is dense and results-heavy with substantial reliance on qualitative, per-dataset/per-model 'Remarks' rather than a small number of crisp, well-supported claims; core findings are frequently hedged or shown to be inconsistent across models/tasks in the very tables meant to support them (e.g., Mistral vs. Llama vs. RoBERTa best-layer rankings in Table 3).

strengths: Extensive multi-model (RoBERTa-Large, Llama-3.2, Qwen-2.5, Mistral-7B), multi-dataset (8 GLUE tasks) empirical study with 10 seeds per configuration, which is a substantial evaluation effort relative to prior work that studied only a single influence method and smaller models.

The paper tackles a practically important and under-explored question (layer choice for tractable influence estimation in LLMs) and directly challenges a seminal prior claim (Yeh et al. 2022) with both empirical correlation analysis and a theoretical counterexample.

Introduces two simple, well-motivated alternative aggregation strategies (Rank, Vote) that empirically outperform mean aggregation on multiple models/datasets, offering a practically useful improvement over the standard averaging baseline used in influence functions.

Proposes a new evaluation proxy (Noise Detection Rate) that avoids costly retraining and shows moderate-to-strong correlation with downstream filtering performance, particularly under Vote aggregation, addressing a genuine bottleneck in influence-function research (expensive fine-tuning-based evaluation).
Detailed appendices with layer-wise NDR curves, per-layer/method correlation matrices, and full per-dataset accuracy tables provide good transparency and reproducibility support for the claims.
weaknesses: Theorem 5.1 is only an existence proof (there exists some validation point x3 for which cancellation-inclusive influence separates noisy/clean samples better) rather than a general result; it does not show this holds on average or in practice, so it is a fairly weak rebuttal of the original cancellation-effect heuristic, and the proof itself contains informal steps (e.g., unjustified 'without loss of generality' sign assumptions) that reduce its rigor.

The central narrative ('first is not better than last') is somewhat inconsistent with the actual findings, which more consistently point to middle/early-middle attention layers as best, not late layers; RoBERTa in particular shows best performance in the last attention layers, and the framing in the title/abstract oversimplifies a more nuanced, model-dependent pattern.

Results are highly inconsistent across models: for Llama-3.2 1B, none of the influence-based filtering configurations beat the naive Random-removal baseline, which undercuts the paper's broader claims about the value of influence-based layer selection and aggregation, and this important caveat is somewhat buried in the appendix/remarks rather than foregrounded.

NDR/AUC correlations with downstream accuracy are only moderate (0.4–0.7) under standard mean aggregation, and only become reliably strong (0.8–0.9) under the paper's own proposed Vote aggregation; this makes the proxy-metric contribution partly dependent on/entangled with the aggregation contribution, weakening the claim that NDR is a generally reliable proxy for arbitrary influence pipelines.

Evaluation is restricted to GLUE-style classification with synthetic uniform label-flip noise and LoRA-tuned encoder/decoder classifiers up to 7B parameters; it is unclear how well the conclusions transfer to the generation/open-ended tasks that dominate real LLM use, or to larger-scale models, limiting the generality of the 'general patterns of influence estimation as models scale' claim.

The paper does not report or compare the computational overhead of the proposed Rank/Vote aggregation strategies relative to standard mean aggregation, despite computational efficiency being a central motivation of the work.

The very large result tables (Tables 4–6) and dense multi-panel figures make it difficult for readers to extract the core takeaways, and some claims (e.g., 'first or second attention layer groups are generally better') are stated somewhat loosely without a single consolidated cross-model summary metric.

strengths: Extensive empirical study spanning four models of varying scale (RoBERTa-Large, Llama-3.2 1B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B, Mistral 7B) and eight GLUE tasks, with 10 random seeds per configuration and statistical significance testing (Wilcoxon, Friedman), which is considerably more thorough than the single-method, single-small-model study it critiques (Yeh et al., 2022).

Provides both an empirical demonstration (weak/absent Spearman correlation between cancellation score C and downstream accuracy) and a theoretical counterexample (Theorem 5.1) showing cancellation is not a reliable indicator of layer usefulness, directly challenging a seminal prior claim.

Introduces two simple but effective alternative aggregation strategies (Rank and Vote) that consistently improve over standard mean aggregation across several influence functions and models, with clear ablations over the voting hyperparameter k.

Proposes the Noise Detection Rate (NDR) and AUC metrics as cheaper proxies for influence-function evaluation that correlate reasonably well (and strongly under Vote aggregation) with costly retrain-based evaluation, which is practically useful for future influence-function research.

Very extensive appendix with additional experiments (autoregressive/instruction datasets, newer influence methods such as EKFAC/RepSim/Outlier Gradient, layer correlation analyses, sample-level rank trajectories) that substantially strengthens robustness of the core claims and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim in the title ('first is not really better than last') is not uniformly supported: results vary considerably by model (RoBERTa-Large favors later layers, Qwen/Mistral favor early-middle layers, and for Llama-3.2 1B no configuration beats random filtering under mean aggregation), suggesting the true finding is 'best layer is model-dependent' rather than a clean refutation of the prior first/last dichotomy — this is a more modest and less crisp conclusion than the framing suggests.

The theoretical proof of Theorem 5.1 is informal and relies on several unstated simplifying assumptions (e.g., 'without loss of generality' derivation of the TracIn relation, treatment of vectors as scalars a_i, b_i, and an implicit assumption about gradient alignment across validation points) that reduce its rigor as a general theoretical result.

Evaluation is confined to small-scale synthetic noise injection (uniform label flipping) on GLUE with relatively small sample budgets (4500 train/500 val/500 test), which may not reflect realistic detrimental-sample distributions (e.g., adversarial poisoning, subtle biases, or real-world noisy web-scale pretraining data) that motivate influence-function applications in practice.

The five-stage pipeline (fine-tune, select best checkpoint, compute influence, filter 30%, retrain) is computationally heavy and only evaluated at a single filtering threshold (30%); sensitivity to filtering ratio is not systematically studied in the main text.

Presentation is dense with an unusually large appendix (13+ sections) and the main paper leans heavily on referring readers to appendices for core findings (e.g., Llama negative results only fully explained in Appendix M), which hurts self-containment and readability.

Novelty of the aggregation methods (Rank, Vote) is somewhat incremental — rank-based/voting aggregation is a fairly standard technique in ensemble and rank-aggregation literature — and the core contribution is largely a careful re-evaluation/benchmarking study rather than a fundamentally new method or theory.
